title: Chaos Exercises and Failure Hypothesis Library (SRE Program 2026)
author: Aisha Patel
content:
Summary:
This page documents Redwood Inference's formal chaos engineering program for 2026, including a curated Failure Hypothesis Library (FHL), exercise cadence, success criteria tied to SLOs and error budgets, safety guardrails, tooling references, and a lightweight post-exercise review template aligned with our incident review standards. The goal is to proactively validate resilience assumptions, reduce mean time to recovery (MTTR), and surface capacity and operational gaps before customer impact.

Objectives:
- Validate critical SLOs and verify graceful degradation strategies under realistic failure modes.
- Exercise cross-team runbook execution and automation paths (serving runtime, autoscaler, routing).
- Identify capacity bottlenecks and quantify error-budget burn under controlled conditions.
- Produce reproducible artifacts (metrics, traces, runbook notes) for continuous improvement and follow-up work.

Scope and frequency:
- Quarterly full-service game days (company-wide, ~72-hour window for preparation and follow-up).
- Monthly targeted micro-chaos tests (single-service or infra component, low blast radius).
- Ad-hoc pre-release or pre-migration exercises for major changes (e.g., new autoscaler, kernel update, quantization rollout).

Alignment with SLOs and error budgets:
- Every exercise must declare one or more target SLOs it is intended to probe (examples below).
- Error-budget impact is simulated and measured; exercises are stopped if projected burn rate exceeds the emergency threshold (see Safety Guardrails).
- Key SLO examples we use as anchors: 
  - Hosted API availability: 99.95% monthly (goal).
  - 99th-token-latency (p99) for generation endpoint: < 1200ms for short contexts (<= 512 tokens).
  - Embeddings throughput SLO: 95% of requests <= 100ms p95 under baseline load.
  - Latency SLOs are expressed per-route and per-model; exercises must list which route(s)/model(s) are affected.

Failure Hypothesis Library (FHL) — canonical entries:
(Use this table as the source of truth for game-day scenarios. Choose 1–3 hypotheses per exercise.)

| ID | Hypothesis | Target services / systems | Primary metrics to monitor | Expected customer-visible effect | Failure mode controls |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| FHL-01 | Partial GPU node pool failure during peak traffic | Serving runtime (gpu-pool-west), load balancer, autoscaler | request success rate, p95 latency, GPU utilization, queue depth | Increased latency; queued requests; degraded throughput for pinned model versions | Immediate rollback to pinned fallback model; scale up reserved capacity; abort test on >2% sling in availability |
| FHL-02 | Persistent KV-cache corruption leading to incorrect prefixes | KV cache service, prefix cache layer, reranking | output-quality regression metrics, error rate, cache hit ratio | Silent quality regressions causing higher downstream corrections | Disable cache and fall back to cold inference path; test data validation hooks |
| FHL-03 | Control plane latency (DB read/write) causing rollout delays | Deployment API, control-plane DB, plan-apply queue | API latency, deployment success rate, autoscaler lag | Rollouts pause/fail; can cause cascade if automated rollouts backlog | Rate-limit control-plane operations; applied automation circuit breaker |
| FHL-04 | Cross-region network partition between US and EU regions | VPC peering, smart routing service | cross-region request rate, fallback routing activations, error budget burn | Regional traffic surge, increased cross-region egress costs, possible customer SLA impact | Force-routing to local region; enable degraded feature set for restricted customers |
| FHL-05 | Model quantization path regression under long contexts | Runtime quantized kernels, model variant selection | p99 latency, generation correctness (eval prompts), memory pressure | Higher hallucination / truncated responses for long context users | Auto-fallback to full-precision variant; abort if quality delta > threshold |
(Test authors should add new hypotheses to the FHL with clear owner, reproducibility steps, and required preconditions.)

Exercise lifecycle (preparation → execution → review):
1) Proposal (2–3 weeks before):
   - Define hypothesis IDs from FHL, target SLOs, blast radius, test schedule, detection metrics, and abort conditions.
   - Register on the Chaos Calendar (internal calendar) and notify affected teams.
   - Pre-authorize capacity reserves (if test needs additional burst capacity).
2) Pre-flight checklist (72 hours before):
   - Verify metric dashboards and runbook links are available.
   - Confirm on-call coverage and communication channel (Slack #chaos-exercises).
   - Create one-click kill switches and API toggles for the test.
3) Execution window (≤ 4 hours for targeted tests; ≤ 6 hours for full-service micro-games):
   - Monitor SLO and error-budget dashboards continuously.
   - Keep an operations lead (OL) and a safety officer (SO) assigned.
4) Abort and rollback: follow abort conditions strictly (see Safety Guardrails).
5) Post-exercise review (within 5 business days):
   - Complete the Post-Exercise Report and action items in JIRA.
   - Add reproducible scripts and artifacts to the FHL entry.

Roles & responsibilities:
- Exercise owner: drafts hypothesis, runs the test, collects artifacts. (Typically Reliability or Platform team engineer).
- Operations lead (OL): monitors KPIs during the test and triggers rollback if thresholds are exceeded.
- Safety officer (SO): has unilateral authority to abort exercises immediately.
- Observability owner: ensures dashboards and traces are collecting the required signals.
- Product/customer success liaison: assesses customer-impact risk and communicates external messaging if necessary.

Safety guardrails (mandatory):
- Abort on: projected monthly error-budget burn rate > 25% (based on observed short-window burn extrapolation), or SLO breach > 5% absolute for critical routes for > 10 minutes.
- No experiments against customer-managed private deployments unless explicit customer approval and a signed change request.
- All experiments must have an accessible kill switch (Slack command + automation runbook).
- Low-blast defaults: start with canary subset (1% traffic) and ramp only with explicit OL approval.

Metrics, dashboards and alerting (operational tooling):
- Required dashboards for every exercise: SLO burn dashboard, request success + error classification, latency distribution (p50/p95/p99), resource utilization (GPU/CPU/Memory), autoscaler events, deployment events.
- Alerting hooks: automated alert when rolling 5m error rate implies >10% of monthly error-budget burn if sustained.
- Tracing: include a correlation id header (X-Game-Day-ID) on all injected traffic to filter traces and logs.

Runbook integration and automation examples:
- Example abort command (via Ops CLI):
  rwn ops abort-game --id GAME-2026-013 --reason "p99 latency > safety-threshold"
- Example scale-up automation (Kubernetes/GPU autoscaler):
  kubectl patch hpa serving-gpu-pool-west -p '{"spec":{"minReplicas":10}}' --namespace serving
- Playbook snippet to fallback a model route to a smaller variant:
  1. Pause traffic routing: curl -X POST https://control-plane.internal/api/route/pause -d '{"route":"/v1/generate","reason":"game-day rollback"}'
  2. Update route to fallback model: PATCH /api/route/{id} body {"model":"redwood-fast-quant-v1"}
  3. Verify success rate and p95 latency, then unpause.

Evidence and post-exercise review template (aligns with incident review standards):
- Title: [GAME-ID] — short hypothesis summary
- Owner: name and team
- Start / stop timestamps (UTC)
- Hypothesis IDs from FHL
- SLOs and metrics targeted (explicit numeric goals)
- Raw artifacts: dashboards links, traces, logs, experiment scripts, correlated request ids
- Outcome: pass / partial / fail (with measuring criteria)
- Root causes (if any issues surfaced) and contributing factors
- Action items (JIRA links) with owners and due dates
- Follow-up test plan (if partial or fail)

Templates and artifacts to attach:
- Metric extraction query examples (Prometheus/ClickHouse/Tempo): include example queries in the exercise doc.
- Experiment scripts (bash/python) stored in repo: infra/chaos/2026/<game-id>/.
- Screenshot checklist for dashboards to capture at t=0, t=mid, t=end.

Tooling (recommended & supported):
- In-house automation runner (rwn-chaos) — preferred for low-blast experiments; integrates with Redwood control plane and kill switches.
- Gremlin / Litmus — approved for deep-failure injection on infra-layer only.
- Grafana / Prometheus / ClickHouse / Tempo for metrics and traces.
- ChatOps integration (Slack) for one-click abort and status updates.

Capacity and cost considerations:
- If an exercise requires reserved capacity changes, coordinate with Capacity Planning and Finance for temporary credits.
- Run a pre-test capacity simulation that projects autoscaler behavior and expected token throughput. Capture these projections in the proposal.

Common anti-patterns (and what to avoid):
- Running large-blast experiments without a designated SO.
- Not pre-registering rollback paths or lacking a kill switch.
- Focusing purely on latency without validating output quality (for inference services both are critical).

Success criteria and KPIs for the chaos program (quarterly review):
- Number of documented hypotheses exercised per quarter >= 6.
- Mean time to abort (MTTA) for tests with issues < 2 minutes (target).
- Percentage of exercises that produce at least one actionable ticket: >= 70%.
- Reduction in mean time to detect (MTTD) for production incidents correlated to exercised failure modes (measured across quarters).

Governance and change control:
- Major changes to the FHL (new classes of failure, long-lived mitigations) require signoff from Reliability leadership.
- All artifacts and tests must be recorded in the Chaos Calendar and linked to a JIRA epic for traceability.

Next steps / checklist for exercise owners:
- Pick FHL entries and complete Proposal template 2 weeks before window.
- Engage Observability owner to validate dashboards 72 hours prior.
- Upload experiment scripts to infra/chaos repo and link in the proposal.
- Run a dry-run in staging using the same correlation headers and collection mechanisms.

Appendix — quick runbook snippets and PromQL examples:
- PromQL: 1m error rate for route /v1/generate:
  sum(rate(http_requests_total{route="/v1/generate",code!~"2.."}[1m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{route="/v1/generate"}[1m]))
- PromQL: estimated month burn projection based on 5m window:
  (current_window_burn * (30*24*60*60) / window_seconds) where window_seconds=300
